message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree:

| Taxonomic level | Lion | Zebra |
|-----------------|------|-------|
| Class | Mammalia | Mammalia |
| Sub‑class | Theria | Theria |
| Infraclass | Eutheria (placentals) | Eutheria |
| Super‑order | Laurasiatheria | Laurasiatheria |
| Order | Carnivora (Feliformia) | Perissodactyla |
| Family | Felidae | Equidae |

Because they diverge at the order level, their most recent common ancestor (MRCA) is the MRCA of the two orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor is a **Laurasiatherian placental mammal** that lived roughly **90–100 million years ago** during the Late Cretaceous/early Paleogene. It would have been a small, generalized mammal—much more primitive than either modern lion or zebra.

In other words, the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of all Laurasiatherian mammals, a basal placental mammal that existed around 90 Myr ago.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a mammalian ancestor that lived around 90-100 million years ago. But maybe the answer: "The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived about 90 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals" if they want a more general answer. But likely they want the last common ancestor of the two species: "the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived around 90 million years ago."
